assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and realised with strontium and ytterbium, brought optical atomic clocks to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. The idea is simple and original: trap the atoms so that the light shift cancels. The clocks now probe gravitational time dilation across millimetres, test fundamental constants and are a leading candidate for a redefinition of the second. This is basic atomic physics that is also precision science, and it is a field I know well.
assessment.attribution: Katori made the decisive proposal and the first demonstrations; Ye's group carried the performance to the frontier and built the comparisons and applications. The two-name credit is clean and fair. As far as I recall, others such as Lemonde, Takamoto and Hall also contributed, but they are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Strong. Many independent laboratories on several continents reproduce and improve the clocks, and the underlying idea is stable. Adjacent prizes (Hall and Hänsch 2005, Wineland and Haroche 2012) make this a natural next step and timely rather than premature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as a distinct discovery or as a continuation of the precision-timekeeping line already honoured.
Ye's contributions span clocks, combs and molecules, so the scope of his citation could be contested; I have not verified details of the early priority history.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling mechanical oscillators to their quantum ground state and controlling them there takes quantum mechanics into massive objects. It speaks directly to where the boundary lies between the quantum and classical worlds, which to me is the most interesting question on this list. It also underpins quantum transduction and sensing at the standard quantum limit.
assessment.attribution: Cleland and colleagues achieved ground-state and single-phonon control in a piezoelectric resonator; Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg developed cavity optomechanics, sideband cooling and the quantum regime in optical systems. These are distinct routes, so the credit is fair but the discovery is somewhat compound.
assessment.maturity: Fairly strong. Several platforms have confirmed ground-state control independently. No single experiment is decisive and the field is still moving, so it may be slightly early.
uncertainties: A compound discovery in which the platforms differ; the committee might favour one route.
Proximity to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits could affect timing.
Others (for example Martinis, Painter, Lehnert, Teufel) made decisive contributions that this credit list omits; I am recalling these from memory and have not checked them.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, including the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and quantum gas microscopes with single-site resolution. This gives a controlled window on many-body quantum physics and has become a standard quantum simulator with real insight into strongly correlated matter.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the Mott-insulator realisation; Greiner and Bloch carried out the key experiments and microscopy. Cirac is also credited for the wider simulation programme, but Bloch, Greiner and Zoller seem the most defensible trio. Jaksch and Hänsch are not on the credited list.
assessment.maturity: Mature: over twenty years of reproduction by many groups and comparison with theory and numerics. Timely.
uncertainties: Whether a prize would be framed as quantum simulation in general or this specific discovery; the theory-experiment split is a real choice.
Cirac might be preferred to Greiner in a different configuration.
The advantage over classical numerics is still limited in some regimes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms is a clear example of quantum mechanics put to work. It gives precise measurements of gravity, rotation and the fine-structure constant, and tests of the equivalence principle. The idea is clean: atoms interfere like light.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard built early atom interferometers with gratings; Bordé gave the theoretical basis (Ramsey-Bordé interferometer); Kasevich built the high-precision light-pulse devices. Others, including Chu, Mlynek and Chebotayev, were also early contributors, which complicates the allocation of credit.
assessment.maturity: Mature in technique, with several precision measurements reproduced, but the most ambitious applications (space-based tests, gravitational-wave detection) have not yet been realised.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier prizes for laser cooling (1997) and separated oscillatory fields (1989).
Several parallel inventors make a three-name allocation contestable.
Fundamental-physics applications are still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics transplanted cavity QED to superconducting circuits, reaching strong coupling and enabling dispersive readout and much of the architecture of superconducting qubits. Conceptually it is an artificial atom coupled to a photon, and it gives a very controllable test bed for quantum optics.
assessment.attribution: The foundational theory proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the first strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff, Schoelkopf and colleagues) are both credited. Four names are listed and at most three can be proposed, so Girvin must be left out, a hard choice.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely reproduced; it is the backbone of a large industry. The 2025 prize in superconducting circuits makes the timing delicate.
uncertainties: Recency of the 2025 prize in the same hardware family.
Theory versus experiment allocation (Blais and Girvin versus Wallraff and Schoelkopf) is unresolved.
Part of the significance is technological rather than a new fundamental discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade gives strong controllable interactions between neutral atoms, and programmable tweezer arrays of hundreds of atoms are used for quantum simulation, entanglement and gates. It combines atomic structure with many-body physics and reveals new phases and dynamics.
assessment.attribution: Lukin's group proposed fast Rydberg gates and demonstrated large programmable arrays; Browaeys and Grangier observed blockade experimentally; Saffman contributed gate proposals and experiments. Four names are credited and the distinctions are delicate.
assessment.maturity: Fairly young. Many groups reproduce key results, but the significance of the quantum simulation results is still being tested against classical simulation. Possibly premature.
uncertainties: Whether quantum advantage claims will hold up remains open.
Credit among Lukin, Browaeys, Saffman, Grangier and others is not settled.
Timing: a few years earlier than the lattice-clock and lattice-simulation candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry's geometric phase show that potentials and geometry have physical consequences, a deep point in quantum mechanics that runs through molecular, condensed-matter and optical physics. The conceptual significance and originality are very high.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959) and Berry (1984) are the natural names, but Bohm is deceased and not on the credited list, and Ehrenberg and Siday anticipated the effect while Pancharatnam anticipated the phase. The two credited living names are a defensible pair, though the combination of two distinct discoveries is a little artificial.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and experimentally confirmed (for example by Tonomura and many others). The concern is the age of the discovery and whether recognition now is timely.
uncertainties: Priority issues (Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam) complicate attribution.
Two related but separate discoveries are combined in one candidate.
The committee may prefer more recent work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube observed a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and later associated neutrinos with a blazar and the Galactic plane, opening neutrino astronomy. It is a new window on the universe built on an ambitious instrument in the Antarctic ice.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led IceCube; Karle was a key figure in its construction and analysis. Yoshida and others also contributed. The collaboration is very large, so any individual allocation is somewhat artificial.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature: the diffuse flux is established by several analyses and the Galactic-plane result adds weight. Individual source identification rests on few events.
uncertainties: I defer to colleagues on astroparticle physics and am not certain of the details of the source evidence.
Source associations rest on small event numbers.
A large collaboration makes the choice of laureates difficult.
